Professor Okafor, do you have a few minutes? I'm having second thoughts about my research topic.
Of course. You were going to look at recycling habits in student housing, right?
Yes, but after reading more, I realized several studies have already covered it in detail. I'm worried I won't add anything new.
That's a reasonable concern. Have you considered narrowing the focus instead of starting over? For example, you could compare dorms that use different bin designs.
Hmm, I hadn't thought of that. That would let me keep the survey I already wrote.
Exactly. You'd just need to add a few questions about the bins. And it's a practical question—the housing office might even be interested in your results.
That makes me feel much better. I'll revise my proposal and send it to you by Friday.
Hi, I just got an email saying I owe a fine for a book that's three weeks overdue, but I'm sure I returned it.
Let me look it up. Which book was it?
It's a statistics textbook. I put it in the return box outside the building on a Sunday.
I see. The return box was out of service for a few days last month because the lock was broken. Some books were placed in the box by mistake and weren't checked in right away.
So the book might still be somewhere in the library?
Most likely. I'll ask our staff to search the back room. If we find it, the fine will be removed automatically.
Great. Should I do anything in the meantime?
No, but please use the front desk for returns until the box is repaired.
Hi, Dr. Chen. I wanted to ask your advice about my lab partner.
Sure. Is something wrong?
Well, he keeps missing our lab sessions, so I end up doing most of the experiments myself. I don't mind the work, but I'm worried our shared report will suffer.
I appreciate you telling me. Have you talked to him directly?
I sent him a message, but he only said he's been busy with his job.
I see. Here's what I'll do. For the next report, each of you will write a separate analysis section. That way your grade reflects your own work.
That sounds fair. Should I keep doing the experiments with him?
Yes, but let me know if he misses another session, and I'll speak with him myself.
Hi. I'm planning to study in Spain next spring, and I want to make sure my courses there will count toward my degree.
Good thinking. Many students wait until they come back, and then they discover some credits don't transfer.
That's what I'm afraid of. I found three courses I'd like to take, but I'm not sure about the economics one.
For major courses, you'll need approval from your department, not just from our office. Bring the course description and the syllabus to your adviser.
What if the syllabus isn't available yet?
Then ask the university in Spain for last year's version. Departments usually accept that as long as the content hasn't changed much.
Okay, I'll email them today.

Attention, students. This Thursday's career fair has been moved from the gymnasium to the student center because of a scheduling conflict. Over forty companies will attend, including several engineering and technology firms that are hiring summer interns. We strongly recommend bringing printed copies of your résumé, as some employers will not accept digital versions. If you'd like feedback on your résumé before the fair, the career office is offering fifteen-minute review sessions on Tuesday and Wednesday afternoons. Sign up on the career office website.

Good morning, residents. Starting next Monday, our dormitory will begin a new food-waste collection program. Green bins will be placed in each kitchen for fruit and vegetable scraps, coffee grounds, and eggshells. Please do not put meat, plastic, or paper towels in these bins, as they cannot be composted. The collected waste will be turned into compost for the campus garden. Our goal is to reduce the amount of trash sent to landfills by thirty percent this year. Thank you for your cooperation.

Welcome to the first event of this year's Science and Society lecture series. Before we begin, a few announcements. Tonight's talk will be recorded and posted online within a week, so if you have friends who couldn't attend, please let them know. After the lecture, there will be a twenty-minute question-and-answer session. Because of time limits, we ask that you keep questions brief and avoid making long statements. Finally, our next speaker, a marine biologist, has had to postpone her visit, so the November event will now take place in early December. Updated details will be emailed to everyone on our mailing list.

May I have your attention, please. The final exam will begin in ten minutes. Please place all bags at the front of the room and make sure your phones are completely turned off, not just silenced. Any device that makes a sound during the exam will result in an automatic penalty. You may keep a clear water bottle on your desk, but no food is allowed. If you finish early, you may leave quietly during the first ninety minutes, but not during the final fifteen minutes, so that students who are still working are not disturbed. Please write your student number, not your name, on every page.

Today I'd like to talk about how habits form. Researchers often describe a habit as a loop with three parts: a cue, a routine, and a reward. The cue is a trigger—say, feeling tired in the afternoon. The routine is the behavior, like buying a coffee. And the reward is the feeling that follows, perhaps more energy or a short break from work. Over time, the brain begins to connect the cue directly with the reward, so the behavior becomes almost automatic. Now, here's the interesting part. Studies suggest that it's very difficult to simply erase a habit. A more effective strategy is to keep the same cue and reward but replace the routine. So instead of buying coffee, you might take a short walk. You still get a break, but the behavior is healthier. One more thing: contrary to popular belief, habits don't form in exactly twenty-one days. In one study, it took participants anywhere from about two months to more than eight months.

Let's look at how some islands are formed. The Hawaiian Islands, for example, sit in the middle of the Pacific Plate, far from any plate boundary. So why are there volcanoes there? Geologists explain this with the idea of a hot spot—a plume of extremely hot material rising from deep within the Earth. As the plate moves slowly over the hot spot, magma breaks through the crust and builds a volcano. Over millions of years, the plate carries that volcano away, and a new one forms over the hot spot. That's why the Hawaiian Islands form a chain, with the oldest islands in the northwest and the youngest, the Big Island, in the southeast. The older islands are also smaller and more eroded, because they're no longer receiving fresh lava. In fact, a new volcano is already forming underwater southeast of the Big Island. It won't reach the surface for tens of thousands of years, though.

Companies spend enormous amounts of money choosing colors for their products and logos. Why? Research suggests that people form a first impression of a product within about ninety seconds, and color plays a major role in that judgment. However, I want to be careful here, because many popular claims about color are oversimplified. You may have read that blue always signals trust or that red always increases excitement. The reality is more complicated. The effect of a color depends heavily on context and on whether it seems to fit the product. A bright pink might work well for a toy but seem strange for a bank. Culture matters too: white is associated with weddings in some countries and with mourning in others. So rather than looking for one perfect color, marketers are better off testing how well a color matches the personality of their brand and the expectations of their customers.

Many structures built by the ancient Romans are still standing after two thousand years, while some modern concrete begins to crack within decades. For a long time, scientists weren't sure why. Recent studies of Roman harbor walls have provided some answers. The Romans mixed lime with volcanic ash, and when seawater soaked into the structures, it triggered chemical reactions that formed new minerals. These minerals actually filled small cracks and made the material stronger over time. Researchers also found small white chunks of lime in Roman concrete. These were once thought to be signs of poor mixing, but now it appears they may have helped the concrete repair itself when water entered a crack. Modern engineers are interested in these findings because self-repairing concrete could make buildings last longer and reduce the large carbon emissions associated with producing new cement.
